content: The inhalation of the enzyme dornase alfa is known to reduce the viscosity of sputum and improve clinical outcomes in individuals with cystic fibrosis. This study aimed to evaluate whether the timing of dornase alfa inhalation—either in relation to airway clearance techniques or based on the time of day (morning versus evening)—affects clinical efficacy, both objectively and subjectively. To address this, randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials were identified through various databases, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro), clinical trial registries, and international cystic fibrosis conference proceedings. The most recent search was conducted on October 12, 2020. Trials were included if they specifically randomized participants based on the timing of dornase alfa inhalation, either before versus after airway clearance techniques or in the morning versus evening. Two independent authors selected the trials, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and meta-analyses were performed where possible. A total of 115 trial reports representing 55 trials were identified, but only five trials (involving 122 participants) met the inclusion criteria. All five trials employed a cross-over design, with intervention periods ranging from two to eight weeks. Four trials (98 participants) compared dornase alfa inhalation before versus after airway clearance techniques. The results showed that inhaling dornase alfa after airway clearance did not significantly alter forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), based on very-low-quality evidence. Similarly, forced vital capacity (FVC) and quality of life were not significantly affected, based on lowand very-low-quality evidence, respectively. However, forced expiratory flow at 25% of the pulmonary volume (FEF25%) was significantly worse when dornase alfa was inhaled after airway clearance. This finding was based on pooled data from two small trials involving children aged 7 to 19 years with well-preserved lung function, showing a mean difference of -0.17 liters (95% confidence interval: -0.28 to -0.05). All other secondary outcomes were statistically non-significant. One trial (25 participants) compared morning versus evening inhalation of dornase alfa and found no significant differences in lung function or symptoms, based on low-quality evidence. The authors concluded that the current evidence, derived from a small number of participants, does not strongly support the notion that inhaling dornase alfa after airway clearance techniques is more or less effective than the traditional recommendation of inhaling it 30 minutes prior to airway clearance. For children with well-preserved lung function, inhalation before airway clearance may offer some benefit for small airway function compared to inhalation after. However, this finding is based on a measure with high variability and trials with inconsistent follow-up periods. In the absence of robust evidence favoring one timing regimen over another, the timing of dornase alfa inhalation can be determined based on practical considerations or individual preferences regarding the timing of airway clearance and the time of day. Further research is needed to provide more definitive guidance.
